title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Criminals are using generative AI to create convincing impersonations of real people for financial fraud. They deploy deepfakes and voice cloning to target vulnerable populations, including immigrants seeking legal services and individuals approached for investment or romance schemes. The impersonation happens at the point of contact, where victims cannot distinguish synthetic media from authentic communication.

This is a deployment of generative AI outside any legitimate use case, in the hands of bad actors rather than the companies that built these systems. Detection would have required victims to verify identities through independent channels before sending money, and it would have required social media platforms to limit the footage that scammers could use to train voice and likeness models. The scale of losses reported suggests that neither prevention worked at the moment victims made decisions.

It is not established what specific generative AI tools the scammers used, who built them, or what safety measures those tools contained.

summary:
Criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence to create deepfakes and clone voices for scams across Georgia and South Florida. Recent cases include a Cobb County couple losing approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency fraud scheme and a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice and identity were cloned to target vulnerable immigrants. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year out of more than $20 billion in total reported internet crime losses. Florida had 350 AI-related complaints resulting in nearly $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia reported 71 complaints with over $10.4 million in losses.

Scammers use generative AI to make fraudulent schemes more convincing by cloning voices from social media videos, spoofing phone numbers, creating fake photographs, and researching family relationships. The technology is making traditional scams like romance schemes, investment fraud, and grandparent scams harder to detect. Authorities recommend families establish secret code words to verify identity, verify urgent requests by contacting people directly, never send money based solely on phone calls, and report suspected scams to law enforcement and the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center.
